verifyNote: Written from standard UK binocular vision practice. Always check against Dr Sheppard's slides — criteria and normal values vary between textbooks and clinics.

topics.title: Heterophoria and heterotropia
topics.summary: From the week 11 BV essentials lecture: a phoria is a latent deviation held by fusion; a tropia is manifest with both eyes open. The cover test is the only objective test that tells them apart, and the real question with a phoria is whether it's compensated.
keyPoints: Covering one eye dissociates the eyes: fusion stops, so the covered eye moves to its passive position, revealing any phoria.
Tropia on cover/uncover of the other eye: the deviated eye moves to fixate: out for esotropia, in for exotropia, down for hypertropia, up for hypotropia.
Phoria on uncovering: out = esophoria, in = exophoria, down = hyper on that side, up = hypo; phorias are usually similar in size in each eye. Smooth fast recovery suggests compensation.
The alternating cover test reveals the total deviation (as when tired or stressed) and any intermittent tropia; cover/uncover shows the habitual one.
Decompensated phoria can give fixation disparity, measured with the Mallett unit.
Prescription changes affect phorias: more minus can decompensate esophoria, more plus exophoria.
examTraps: Mixing up the direction: the eye moving outwards to take up fixation means it was turned in (eso).
Treating any phoria as abnormal: what matters is compensation and symptoms.

diagram.description: Pairs of eyes viewing a target. Top row (phoria): both eyes straight when uncovered; under a cover the covered eye drifts out (exophoria). Bottom row (tropia): with both eyes open the left eye is turned out (exotropia).
labels: Phoria: straight with both eyes open
Tropia: deviation with both eyes open

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: compensation criteria
goDeeper.body: Sheard's criterion (fusional reserve opposing the phoria should be at least twice the phoria) and Percival's criterion are common ways to judge compensation alongside symptoms and fixation disparity. Decompensated phoria typically causes eyestrain, headaches, blur and intermittent diplopia with sustained tasks.

flashcards.back: Phoria = latent (fusion holds it); tropia = manifest with both eyes open.
A small exophoria at near is normal.

mcq.q: Near exophoria 6Δ, base-out reserve to blur 15Δ. Does it meet Sheard's criterion?

options.feedback: Right: 15Δ ≥ 12Δ.

options.text: No — the reserve must be 3 × the phoria
options.feedback: Sheard uses twice, not three times.

options.text: No — you need the base-in reserve
options.feedback: For exophoria, the opposing reserve is base-out (convergent).
Sheard can be applied on its own.

mcq.explanation: Sheard: compensating (opposing) reserve ≥ 2 × phoria. For exo, the compensating reserve is convergent (base-out).

mcq.q: Near exophoria 12Δ, base-out reserve to blur 12Δ. Sheard prism?

options.feedback: Exophoria is relieved with base-in prism.
Subtract a third of the reserve.
12Δ is less than 2 × 12Δ, so it fails Sheard.

mcq.explanation: Sheard prism = 2/3 phoria − 1/3 reserve; base direction is base in for exo.

topics.askClaude: Give me phoria measurements with fusional reserves and ask me whether each meets Sheard's criterion and what prism (if any) it suggests.

topics.title: The cover test
topics.summary: From the week 11 BV essentials lecture: the cover test is objective and the only test that distinguishes phoria from tropia. Do it in three stages at distance and near, first with the habitual and then the optimal correction.
keyPoints: Set-up: room lights on, a lamp can help you see the eyes, target one line larger than the worse eye's VA (spotlight if worse than about 6/18), primary gaze.
Stage 1, cover/uncover for tropia: cover the left, watch the right for 2–3 seconds; uncover and watch it return; then repeat the other way.
Stage 2, cover/uncover for phoria (only if no tropia): watch the covered eye as it's uncovered; it recovers to the active position.
Stage 3, alternating cover: move the cover quickly between eyes for 10–30 seconds to stop fusion and show the total deviation and any intermittent tropia.
Near: same steps with the near correction, a detailed target on a near stick; consider looking down if there are near symptoms.
Size: estimate (1 cm at 1 m = 1Δ) or neutralise with a prism bar during the alternating cover (base in for exo, base out for eso) to find the objective angle.
examTraps: Doing the alternating cover first: it can break down a phoria before you've checked for a tropia.
Using a light at distance when VA allows letters: you lose control of accommodation.
Getting the prism base direction backwards.

diagram.description: Sequence of four eye pairs: (1) both eyes fixating; (2) right eye covered — left eye stays still (no left tropia); (3) cover removed — right eye moves in from an outward position (exophoria recovery); (4) alternate cover between eyes showing each eye moving in as it's uncovered.

goDeeper.heading: Worked SAQ: right esotropia
goDeeper.body: Cover LE: RE moves out to fixate and LE moves in under the cover (Hering's law). Uncover LE: RE moves back in and LE moves out. Cover RE: no movement. Uncover RE: no movement.

goDeeper.heading: Versional recovery
goDeeper.body: Some patients with large phorias or marked dominance recover with a version (both eyes move) followed by a vergence, which obeys Hering's law, instead of only the covered eye moving.

checklist.title: Cover test routine
steps: Distance target: a letter one or two lines above the worse eye's VA.
Cover the right eye; watch the left for movement (tropia?).
Uncover the right eye; watch it for recovery (phoria direction, speed).
Alternate cover several times; note direction and estimate size.
Measure with a prism bar if needed.
Repeat at near with an accommodative target.
Record direction, size, recovery, distance and near (e.g. 'D: ortho; N: 6Δ XOP, good recovery').

flashcards.front: Test that shows the total deviation

flashcards.back: The covered eye moves inwards to recover.
1 cm at 1 m = 1Δ; or neutralise with a prism bar (base in for exo, base out for eso).

flashcards.front: Which cover test reveals intermittent tropias?

mcq.q: You cover the right eye and the left eye moves inwards to take up fixation. What does this show?

options.feedback: Yes — the left eye was turned out and moved in to fixate.
An esotropic eye would move outwards.
Phoria is seen on the covered eye when uncovering.
Movement on cover–uncover means a tropia.

mcq.explanation: On cover–uncover, a movement of the uncovered eye means it wasn't fixating — a tropia. Inward movement means it was out (exo).

cases.scenario: BVP SAQ: in primary gaze the right eye is turned in.
cases.question: Name the deviation [1] and describe the distance cover/uncover test findings [4].
cases.modelAnswer: Right esotropia [1]. Cover LE: RE moves out to take up fixation, and LE moves in under the cover (Hering's law) [1]. Uncover LE: RE moves back in to its deviated position and LE moves back out [1]. Cover RE: neither eye moves [1]. Uncover RE: neither eye moves [1].

topics.askClaude: Describe what you see during cover tests (which eye moves, which way, on cover or uncover) and ask me to name the deviation each time.

topics.title: Fixation disparity and the Mallett unit
topics.summary: From the week 11 BV essentials lecture: within Panum's fusional area the eyes can be slightly misaligned and still see singly. This fixation disparity is likely with a decompensated phoria, and the Mallett unit measures the aligning prism that removes it.
keyPoints: Panum's fusional area: each retinal point corresponds to an area on the other retina; single vision is kept over a small space in front of and behind the horopter (Panum's fusional space).
Fixation disparity: a small misalignment within Panum's area; exo, eso, hyper or hypo slip.
Aligning prism (once called associated phoria): the prism that removes the fixation disparity.
Near Mallett set-up: polaroid visor over the near Rx, text matching their near VA, check both nonius strips are seen.

Ask if the strips line up with the X; if not, find the smallest base-in prism (exo slip) or base-out prism (eso slip) that aligns them. Repeat with the vertical OXO and vertical prism, and ask about tilt (cyclodeviation).
At near, extra plus can remove an eso slip by reducing accommodative convergence.
examTraps: Asking leading questions ('Is the line moving to the left?').
Confusing the aligning prism with the dissociated phoria from the cover test.

diagram.description: Mallett OXO target: letters O X O in the centre (seen by both eyes), a polarised vertical line above (seen by one eye) and below (seen by the other). Left panel: lines aligned with the X. Right panel: lower line shifted sideways — a horizontal slip.

goDeeper.heading: When are prisms indicated?
goDeeper.body: The answer sheet notes that good prism adaptation argues against prescribing prism for a slip with asthenopia. Consider the slip together with symptoms and other compensation tests.

flashcards.back: A small vergence error within Panum's area that still allows single vision.
The prism that eliminates the Mallett slip (associated phoria).
OXO — seen by both eyes to lock fusion.

mcq.q: A patient has a 10Δ exophoria on the cover test but no Mallett slip and no symptoms. Interpretation?

options.feedback: Yes — no slip and no symptoms.
Dissociated phoria size alone doesn't decide.
The cover test showed a phoria.

options.text: The Mallett unit must be faulty
options.feedback: This combination is common.

mcq.explanation: Compensation depends on how well fusion copes, not the dissociated size. No slip, no symptoms → compensated.

options.text: The near Mallett nonius strips may align if plus lenses are added for a patient with a near eso slip
options.feedback: Yes: less accommodation means less convergence.

options.text: The OXO targets are the only part of the Mallett unit seen monocularly
options.feedback: The OXO is seen binocularly (fusion lock); the nonius strips are seen one by each eye.

options.text: Prism correction is indicated for retinal slip with asthenopia and good prism adaptation
options.feedback: Good prism adaptation argues against prisms.

mcq.explanation: BVP week 11 question and answer sheet.

cases.question: Describe how you'd use the near Mallett unit to investigate fixation disparity and measure aligning prism.
cases.modelAnswer: Set-up (up to 2): polaroid visor over the near Rx; ask them to read text matching their near VA; check both green nonius strips are seen. Then: ask if the strips line up with the X; if not, find the smallest base-in (exo slip) or base-out (eso slip) prism that aligns them [2]; repeat with the vertical OXO using vertical prism [1]; ask whether the strips look tilted (cyclodeviation) [1].

topics.askClaude: Explain fixation disparity and the Mallett unit simply, then give me 3 patients with cover test, Mallett and symptom results and ask what I'd do.

topics.title: Convergence insufficiency
topics.summary: Convergence insufficiency (CI) is a common cause of near-work symptoms: the eyes struggle to converge and hold convergence. Typical signs are a receded near point of convergence, more exophoria at near than distance, and reduced positive fusional reserves at near.
keyPoints: Symptoms with near work: eyestrain, headaches, blur, double vision, words moving, losing place, poor concentration.
Receded near point of convergence (NPC) — clinics often use a break of about 6–10 cm or more as abnormal (check your criteria).
Exophoria greater at near than at distance.
Reduced base-out (positive) fusional reserves at near, often failing Sheard's criterion.
Rule out other causes: uncorrected refractive error, accommodative insufficiency, convergence paresis (neurological).

Treatment: vergence/accommodative therapy — office-based therapy with home reinforcement had the best results in the CITT trials; home exercises (e.g. pencil push-ups, dot card, stereograms) are common first steps.
Base-in prism for near can help some adults but is less effective in children.
examTraps: Measuring NPC with a non-accommodative target.
Forgetting to measure recovery as well as break.
Missing an underlying refractive or accommodative problem.

diagram.description: Side view: an RAF rule with a target moving towards the patient's nose. Both eyes converge until one eye drifts out (break point). The break distance in cm is marked; recovery shown as the target is moved back until both eyes refixate.

goDeeper.heading: Measuring NPC
goDeeper.body: Use a small accommodative target (e.g. a line of print on an RAF rule) at about 40 cm, move it slowly towards the nose and ask the patient to say when it goes double — and watch the eyes. Note the break and the recovery as you move it away. Repeat a few times: a near point that recedes with repetition suggests poor stamina.

goDeeper.heading: Exercises
goDeeper.body: Dot card: a card with dots along a line; patient converges on each dot, keeping it single with the others seen double. Pencil push-ups: follow a target in towards the nose until it doubles, then back. Stereograms and jump convergence build fusional reserves. Keep them short, regular and progress gradually; review after a few weeks.

flashcards.back: Receded NPC, exo greater at near, reduced positive fusional reserves at near.
Office-based vergence/accommodative therapy with home reinforcement.

mcq.q: A 15-year-old has headaches reading, NPC break 14 cm, 2Δ exo at distance and 12Δ exo at near, low base-out reserves. Most likely?

options.feedback: Yes — all three classic signs.
That's more exo at distance.
That's eso at near.
Basic exo is similar at distance and near.

mcq.explanation: Exo greater at near, receded NPC and reduced convergent reserves = CI.

topics.askClaude: Explain how to tell convergence insufficiency from accommodative insufficiency, then quiz me with 3 cases.

topics.title: Prism prescribing basics
topics.summary: Prism moves the image so the eyes don't have to work as hard to fuse. Use it for symptomatic decompensated phorias (and some tropias) when other options aren't enough — usually the smallest amount that relieves symptoms, split between the eyes.
keyPoints: A prism dioptre (Δ) displaces light 1 cm at 1 m.
Images are displaced towards the apex; the eye turns towards the apex.
Exo deviation → base-in prism; eso → base-out; right hyper → base down right (or base up left).
Split horizontal prism equally between the eyes; vertical prism is usually split too (base down one eye, base up the other).
Base on Mallett aligning prism or Sheard/Percival calculations, then trial it in a trial frame.
Prism can be ground in or produced by decentration (Prentice: c (cm) = P ÷ F) if the lens power allows.
Fresnel press-on prisms are useful for trials or temporary needs (but reduce VA and contrast).
examTraps: Prescribing the full dissociated phoria as prism.
Forgetting to check the prism can actually be achieved by decentration with the lens power and blank size.

diagram.description: Two eyes looking through prisms. Exophoria example: base-in prisms in front of each eye (bases towards the nose), with the images displaced outward towards the apices so the eyes don't need to converge as much.

goDeeper.heading: Notation
goDeeper.body: Write prism with power and base direction for each eye, e.g. R 1Δ BI, L 1Δ BI (total 2Δ BI). For vertical: R 1Δ BD, L 1Δ BU (total 2Δ right hyper relieved). Some clinics use 360° base notation; follow your department's format.

goDeeper.heading: Decentration instead of ground prism
goDeeper.body: Prentice: P = cF, so c (cm) = P ÷ F. For 1Δ base in with a −4.00 D lens, c = 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25 cm = 2.5 mm. Direction: a minus lens is thickest at its edge (base away from the OC), so to put base in front of the eye you move the OC outwards (temporally). A plus lens is thickest at its centre (base towards the OC), so for base in you move the OC inwards (nasally). Sketch it to check, and make sure the blank size allows the decentration.

flashcards.front: Which way does the image move through a prism?

flashcards.back: Base down right (or base up left), usually split.

mcq.q: How much decentration gives 2Δ with a +5.00 D lens?

options.feedback: That multiplies instead of divides.
That's for 2Δ with an 8 D lens.
c comes out in cm: 0.4 cm = 4 mm.

mcq.explanation: Prentice's rule rearranged: c (cm) = P ÷ F.

mcq.q: A patient's Mallett unit shows a right hyper slip neutralised by 1Δ. How might you prescribe it?

options.text: R 0.5Δ base down, L 0.5Δ base up
options.feedback: Yes — split, base down over the hyper eye.
Base up in front of the hyper eye makes it worse.

options.text: R 0.5Δ base in, L 0.5Δ base in
options.feedback: That's horizontal prism.

options.text: No prism — vertical prism is never prescribed
options.feedback: Small vertical prisms often help symptomatic patients.

mcq.explanation: A right hyper is relieved by base down right / base up left, usually split between eyes.

topics.askClaude: Quiz me on prism base directions and Prentice's rule decentration, including which way to move the optical centre for plus and minus lenses.
